doc.title: Chico Hamilton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Swing records, mandatory school music, and meeting the bands at the station
summary: He listened to Goodman and Krupa, LA schools required music study, and students were let out of school to meet touring bands at the train station.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Okay, so let’s go back and look at your involvement with music. You say you picked up the clarinet because your buddy Jack was playing it. What kind of music were you listening to and what kind of music were you playing?

There was only one kind of music at that time, which was dynamite, was swing. Man, I’d wake up every morning going to school listening to Benny Goodman, right, (musical sounds) Don’t Be That Way, and Gene Krupa used to (musical sounds). First of all man, that was the beautiful thing about LA, the educational system. The requirement you had to take some form of music, either it was playing an instrument, whatever, music theory or whatever, listening or whatever. You had to be involved with some kind of music before you could graduate even from grade school And what they used to do, when all the bands used to come to LA, Duke, Basie, Jimmie Lunceford, Benny Goodman, they used to let us out of school to go down to the train station and meet the bands, you know, and it was super.
So what did you do when you went to meet the band? You would stand on the platform when they came off?
You know, just idolized them, you know.
Did you run up and get their autograph?
Oh, yeah. No, I didn’t get an autograph. I was too bashful for that but we used to go down -­
To see that on tape, Chico Hamilton, bashful, back then.
